what: 4. Estimating the exposure effect from your own data
title: Air pollution: dispersion, health burden, equity, and the footprint of the computation
text: individual area data confounders available, partially linear model Chernozhukov et al. (2018) estimates exposure effect cross-fitted nuisance functions, confounder adjustment overfit rows evaluated . exposure_response_plr() adds percentile bootstrap sensitivity interval. default estimator uses ordinary-least-squares nuisances; estimator interface can passed. true coefficient 0.3 interval covers .
code: set.seed(1) n <- 300 sim <- data.frame(income = rnorm(n), density = rnorm(n)) sim$no2 <- 20 - 2 * sim$income + 3 * sim$density + rnorm(n) sim$asthma_rate <- 5 + 0.3 * sim$no2 - 0.5 * sim$income + rnorm(n) fit <- exposure_response_plr(sim, outcome = "asthma_rate", exposure = "no2",                              confounders = c("income", "density"), n_bootstrap = 30) c(ate = fit$ate, lower = fit$ci_lower_bs, upper = fit$ci_upper_bs) #>       ate     lower     upper  #> 0.2464713 0.1437978 0.3132657

title: Attestations, signed bundles and tamper-evident chains
text: attestation binds signature manifest manifest covers, optional note person signing: verifier needs attestation manifest, nothing else. change manifest breaks , presenting different key: key_expected reader pins signer: attestation carries public key made , reader knows key expect say , key .
code: m <- make_manifest(list(dataset = "otis", rows = 1200L), environment = FALSE) key <- fips_keygen("ML-DSA-65") att <- capsule_attest(m, key, note = "counts as published")  res <- capsule_check_attestation(att, m) res$ok #> [1] TRUE res$checks #>                  check   ok #> 1 attestation_complete TRUE #> 2      manifest_digest TRUE #> 3            signature TRUE #>                                                             detail #> 1                                                                  #> 2 efa1b7387f225380245de0b5170999e87ad4044f3e8fd2ef6a6bfbc2bd0a9c90 #> 3 m2 <- m m2$meta$rows <- 1201L capsule_check_attestation(att, m2)$ok #> [1] FALSE  capsule_check_attestation(att, m, key_expected = fips_keygen("ML-DSA-65")$public)$ok #> [1] FALSE

title: Attestations, signed bundles and tamper-evident chains

code: dir <- tempfile() dir.create(dir) write.csv(data.frame(x = 1:3), file.path(dir, "data.csv"), row.names = FALSE) m <- make_manifest(list(dataset = "demo"), environment = FALSE) key <- fips_keygen("ML-DSA-44")  b <- capsule_bundle(dir, m, key, note = "as published") capsule_bundle_verify(attr(b, "path"), dir, manifest = m)$ok #> [1] TRUE write.csv(data.frame(x = 1:4), file.path(dir, "data.csv"), row.names = FALSE) v <- capsule_bundle_verify(attr(b, "path"), dir, manifest = m) v$ok #> [1] FALSE capsule_bundle_read(attr(b, "path"))$attestation$note #> [1] "as published" unlink(dir, recursive = TRUE)

title: Categorical integrity: labels that cannot be swapped quietly
text: recode_manifest() writes mapping digest, counts , checks passed, , key, signature record. later reader verifies file data. Change data file afterwards verification says , reason. Finally, guard stops factor reaching numeric treatment slot, .numeric() hand model level indices instead data:
code: key <- pqc_keygen(height = 2) m <- recode_manifest(x, y, c(W = "White", B = "Black", I = "Indigenous"),                      published = c(White = 2, Black = 2, Indigenous = 1),                      key = key, context = "vignette") p <- write_recode_manifest(m, tempfile(fileext = ".json")) verify_recode_manifest(p, x, y)[c("ok", "signature_ok")] #> $ok #> [1] TRUE #>  #> $signature_ok #> [1] TRUE y_swapped <- as.character(y) y_swapped[y_swapped == "Black"] <- "Indigenous" verify_recode_manifest(p, x, y_swapped)[c("ok", "reasons")] #> $ok #> [1] FALSE #>  #> $reasons #> [1] "verify_recode: ‘B’ was mapped to ‘Indigenous’ but the declared mapping says ‘Black’. THIS is how groups get swapped; fix the recode before any model runs." #> [2] "recoded counts differ from the manifest" guard_binary(c("treated", "control"), "treatment") #> Error: #> ! Column ‘treatment’ is categorical (‘treated’, ‘control’...). Refusing to coerce: as.numeric() on a factor returns level INDICES (1, 2, ...), not your data, and a mis-ordered level silently relabels every observation. Encode explicitly first, e.g. guard_recode() + as.integer(x == "treated_label").

code: observed <- c(White = "Black", Black = "Other", Other = "Unknown", Unknown = "White") relabel_forensics(code_book, observed) #> Mechanism(s) reproducing the observed permutation: #>   * labels sorted alphabetically, assigned by code position #>       White -> Black, Black -> Other, Other -> Unknown, Unknown -> White #>   * labels sorted case-insensitively, assigned by code position #>       White -> Black, Black -> Other, Other -> Unknown, Unknown -> White #>   * rotation by 1 position(s) #>       White -> Black, Black -> Other, Other -> Unknown, Unknown -> White #>  #> The observed permutation is reproduced EXACTLY by: labels sorted alphabetically, assigned by code position; labels sorted case-insensitively, assigned by code position; rotation by 1 position(s). No import routine (haven, foreign, pandas, pyreadstat) reorders value labels; each carries them keyed by code. A transfer fault does not select the sort order of the labels. The step that did this was a positional relabel in the analysis, and it is reproducible from the code book alone.

title: Hawkes processes: self-exciting event series
text: Ogata’s thinning algorithm simulates process exactly: propose events upper bound intensity keep probability λ(t)/λmax\lambda(t)/\lambda_{\max}. exponential kernel ϕ(s)=αβe−βs\phi(s) = \alpha \beta e^{-\beta s}, whose branching ratio α\alpha:
code: simulate_hawkes <- function(mu, alpha, beta, horizon, seed = 1) {   set.seed(seed)   t <- 0   events <- numeric(0)   while (t < horizon) {     lambda_max <- mu + alpha * beta * sum(exp(-beta * (t - events)))     t <- t + stats::rexp(1, lambda_max)     if (t >= horizon) break     lambda_t <- mu + alpha * beta * sum(exp(-beta * (t - events)))     if (stats::runif(1) <= lambda_t / lambda_max) events <- c(events, t)   }   events } times <- simulate_hawkes(mu = 1, alpha = 0.5, beta = 2, horizon = 300) length(times) #> [1] 559

title: Hawkes processes: self-exciting event series
text: core_hawkes_fit() maximises exact log-likelihood analytic gradient C (projected BFGS, parameters bounded). theta holds baseline, branching ratio kernel parameter: branching ratio recovered close 0.5 data simulated , baseline close 1. Four kernels available: exponential (memoryless decay), weibull gamma (delayed peak), lomax (heavy tail: influence fades slowly). Compare information criterion: sinusoidal baseline lets background rate follow cycle (weekly seasonal pattern) instead staying constant:
code: fit <- core_hawkes_fit(times, horizon = 300, kernel = "exponential") fit$theta #> [1] 0.1027148 0.4073514 2.1590220 fit$branching_ratio #> [1] 0.4073514 sapply(c("exponential", "weibull", "lomax"), function(k) {   core_hawkes_fit(times, 300, kernel = k)$aic }) #> exponential     weibull       lomax  #>    352.1139    353.6296    354.1802 core_hawkes_fit(times, 300, kernel = "exponential", baseline = "sinusoidal")$aic #> [1] 352.3058

code: library(rmoriebricklayer) otis <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "otis_a01_individuals.csv",                              package = "rmoriebricklayer")) a <- analyse_table(otis, value = "individuals", period = "year",                    by = c("table", "group"), rounding = 5) a                                   # what changed, how sure, what was withheld report_analysis(a, "otis.html")     # one self-contained file library(rmoriebricklayer)  # 1. The pin: portal endpoint, resource pattern, expected schema, recipe. prov_path <- file.path(tempdir(), "data_provenance.json") writeLines('{   "dataset": {     "title": "Demo library statistics",     "ckan_api_endpoint": "https://data.ontario.ca/api/3/action/package_show?id=ontario-public-library-statistics"   },   "resource": { "name_match_pattern": "2014" },   "schema": {     "expected_columns": ["year", "visits", "alert"],     "structural_invariants": { "min_data_rows": 5 },     "expected_value_sets": { "year": [2024, 2025] },     "synthetic_recipe": {       "n_rows": 25, "seed": 42,       "columns": {         "year":   { "type": "sample",    "values": [2024, 2025] },         "visits": { "type": "poisson",   "lambda": 3, "min": 1 },         "alert":  { "type": "bernoulli", "p": 0.2 },         "id":     { "type": "id_pattern", "pattern": "p-{seq:05d}" }       }     }   } }', prov_path) prov <- load_provenance(prov_path)  # 2. The data. With network: resolve the pinned endpoint to a current URL and #    download (Wayback fallback). Without: a reproducible stand-in from the #    recipe, marked synthetic all the way through. #   url  <- resolve_via_ckan(prov) #   path <- friendly_download(url, file.path(tempdir(), "data.csv")) path <- file.path(tempdir(), "data.csv") gen  <- make_synthetic_csv(prov$schema$synthetic_recipe, path)  # 3. Integrity and schema. sha256_file(path)                               # pin this in the provenance df     <- read.csv(path) issues <- validate_schema(df, prov)             # names, types, value sets, rows  # 4. The manifest: named cross-checks, then the two capsule artifacts. man <- make_manifest(list(project = "my-study", synthetic = TRUE)) man <- record(man, "rows", observed = nrow(df), expected = gen$rows,               synthetic = TRUE) write_manifest_json(man, file.path(tempdir(), "manifest.json")) write_summary_txt(man, tempdir(),                   paths = list(input = path, results = tempdir()),                   what_was_done = "* validated the schema and recorded the row count") # Did the distribution change, not just the bytes? set.seed(1) ref  <- data.frame(value = rnorm(300), size = runif(300, 1, 10),                    grade = sample(c("a", "b", "c"), 300, TRUE)) same <- data.frame(value = rnorm(300), size = runif(300, 1, 10),                    grade = sample(c("a", "b", "c"), 300, TRUE)) capsule_drift(ref, same)$any_drift        # a fresh draw: FALSE moved <- same moved$size <- moved$size * 3              # a silently rescaled column moved$grade[1:100] <- "z"                 # and a new category capsule_drift(ref, moved)                 # both are caught  # Authenticate the manifest so a verifier knows who produced it. digest <- sha256_file(file.path(tempdir(), "manifest.json")) key <- pqc_keygen()                       # post-quantum, hash-based sig <- capsule_sign(digest, key) capsule_verify(digest, sig, signing_public_key(key)) key <- xmss_advance(key, sig)            # the next signature must use this

departs from Benford's law (screen only, not a verdict) #>  #>   values used  2,000 #>   chi-square   769.038 #>   df           8 #>   p-value      <2e-16 #>  #>   digit  observed  expected        shape #>       1     0.106     0.301  #################    #>       2     0.123     0.176  #################### #>       3     0.123     0.125  #################### #>       4     0.112     0.097  ##################   #>       5     0.103     0.079  #################    #>       6     0.102     0.067  #################    #>       7     0.099     0.058  ################     #>       8     0.119     0.051  ###################  #>       9     0.112     0.046  ##################   #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  # The expected proportions are the closed form. b <- benford_test(10^stats::runif(500, 0, 5)) all.equal(b$expected / b$n, log10(1 + 1 / (1:9))) #> [1] "names for target but not for current"  # Zeros carry no leading digit and are excluded from n. benford_test(c(0, 0, 1, 2, 3))$n #> [1] 3  try(benford_test(c(0, NA))) #> Error : `x` has no finite non-zero values to take a leading digit from

an R object, type and attributes included #>   bricklayer_json_to_json        Encode an R object as JSON (jsonlite's toJSON, natively) #>   bricklayer_json_unserialize    JSON serialisation of an R object, type and attributes included #>   json_gzip_decode               Compressed, base64-encoded JSON #>   json_gzip_encode               Compressed, base64-encoded JSON #>   write_manifest_json administrative table in one call #>  #> Description: #>  #>      The questions asked of a published table are always the same: #>      what is in it, what changed between periods and how sure can one #>      be, what the rates are if there is an exposure, whether a short #>      series trends, and whether this release differs from the one #>      held before. Each has a function in this package; this runs them #>      together, with the pieces a reviewer needs and that are easy to #>      forget on a deadline: exact intervals on every change, #>      multiple-comparison adjustment over the groups scanned, the #>      envelope that rounding and suppression in the release imply, and #>      a drift screen against the prior capsule. #>  #> Usage: #>  #>      analyse_table( #>        data, #>        value, #>        period, #>        by = NULL, #>        population = NULL, #>        prior = NULL, #>        units = c("count", "continuous", "percent"), #>        rounding = NULL, #>        rounding_kind = c("nearest", "random"), #>        suppression_limit = NULL, #>        direction = c("neutral", "higher_is_better", "lower_is_better"), #>        per = 1000, #>        conf_level = 0.95, #>        alpha = 0.05, #>        adjust = "BH" #>      ) #>       #> Arguments: #>  #>     data: A data frame in long form: one row per period and group. #>  #>    value: Name of the column (a string) with the published count (or #>           measure). #>  #>   period: Name of the column with the period (fiscal year, quarter, #>           ...); numeric periods are used as the time axis of the #>           trend tests. #>  #>       by: Optional character vector of grouping column names #>           (institution, region, ...). ‘NULL’ (the default) treats the #>           table as one series. #>  #> population: Optional name of an exposure column for rates (‘NULL’, #>           the default, skips the rate step). #>  #>    prior: Optional data frame: the previous capsule of the same #>           table, for the drift screen. ‘NULL’ (the default) skips it. #>  #>    units: ‘"count"’ (the default), ‘"continuous"’ or ‘"percent"’, as #>           in ‘yoy()’. #>  #> rounding, rounding_kind, suppression_limit: How the release rounds or #>           suppresses cells; see ‘published_bounds()’. ‘rounding’ is #>           the rounding base (for example 5), ‘rounding_kind’ #>           ‘"nearest"’ (the default) or ‘"random"’, #>           ‘suppression_limit’ the threshold below which cells are #>           suppressed. ‘NULL’ when the counts are exact. Used only for #>           counts: with other ‘units’ they are ignored, with a #>           warning. #>  #> direction: Which way is an improvement, as in ‘yoy()’: ‘"neutral"’ #>           (the default), ‘"higher_is_better"’ or ‘"lower_is_better"’. #>  #>      per: Rate denominator, as in ‘rate()’; default 1000 (rates per #>           1,000 of ‘population’). #>  #> conf_level: Confidence level for every interval, default 0.95. #>  #>    alpha: Level for the multiple-comparison decision and the drift #>           screens, default 0.05. #>  #>   adjust: Multiple-comparison method for ‘scan_adjust()’, default #>           ‘"BH"’ (Benjamini-Hochberg). #>  #> Details: #>  #>      The steps, in order: #>  #>        1. profile: ‘profile_columns()’ and ‘missingness_summary()’ on #>           ‘data’; #>  #>        2. change: ‘yoy()’ between consecutive periods within each #>           ‘by’ group. For ‘units = "count"’ the exact p-values are #>           then adjusted across all comparisons with ‘scan_adjust()’, #>           and, when ‘rounding’ or ‘suppression_limit’ is given, #>           ‘yoy_bounds()’ adds the publication envelope (see #>           ‘published_bounds()’). For ‘"continuous"’ and ‘"percent"’ #>           units neither step runs: ‘rounding’ and ‘suppression_limit’ #>           are then ignored, with a warning; #>  #>        3. rates (only with ‘population’): ‘rate()’ per group and #>           period, and ‘rate_change()’ between periods, adjusted with #>           ‘scan_adjust()’; #>  #>        4. trend: per group, the values summed within each period, #>           then ‘trend_test()’ (Mann-Kendall tau, p-value and #>           Theil-Sen slope) and, for counts, ‘count_trend()’ (Poisson #>           rate ratio per period). A group with fewer than three #>           periods gets ‘NA’; a test that fails gets ‘NA’ rather than #>           an error; #>  #>        5. drift (only with ‘prior’): ‘capsule_drift()’ of ‘data’ #>           against ‘prior’. #>  #>      Nothing is written and nothing is fetched; a progress bar for #>      the trend step is drawn on stderr unless ‘options(morie.quiet = #>      TRUE)’. Errors: ‘data’ or ‘prior’ not a data frame; a named #>      column not in ‘data’; an invalid ‘units’, ‘direction’ or #>      ‘rounding_kind’; a ‘conf_level’ outside (0, 1); and any error of #>      the functions called (for example negative counts in ‘yoy()’). #>  #> Value: #>  #>      A list of class ‘bricklayer_analysis’ (with a print method that #>      summarises it in a few lines): #>  #>      ‘profile’ #>           ‘profile_columns()’ of ‘data’. #>  #>      ‘missingness’ #>           named numeric from ‘missingness_summary()’. #>  #>      ‘change’ #>           the ‘yoy()’ table; for counts with the added columns #>           ‘p_value’, ‘p_adjusted’ and ‘significant’, and with ‘env_*’ #>           and ‘combined_pct_lower’/‘combined_pct_upper’ when #>           publication bounds were requested. #>  #>      ‘rates’, ‘rate_change’ #>           the ‘rate()’ and ‘rate_change()’ tables when ‘population’ #>           is given, otherwise ‘NULL’. #>  #>      ‘trend’ #>           data frame with one row per group: the ‘by’ columns, #>           ‘periods’, ‘first’, ‘last’, ‘tau’, ‘trend_p’, ‘slope’, #>           ‘rate_ratio’, ‘rate_ratio_lower’, ‘rate_ratio_upper’. #>  #>      ‘drift’ #>           ‘capsule_drift()’ result against ‘prior’, or ‘NULL’. #>  #>      ‘meta’ #>           list of the arguments used, ‘n_rows’, the sorted ‘periods’, #>           ‘prior’ (logical) and ‘when’ (a time stamp). #>  #> See Also: #>  #>      ‘report_analysis()’ writes the result as a Markdown or HTML #>      report. #>   # one verb's usage, and the examples of a help page bricklayer_cli(c("help", "data")) #> usage: rmoriebricklayer data list | data pull db/table [--out FILE.csv]   curated tables at data.rmorie.com (your MORIE key) bricklayer_cli(c("examples", "period_days")) #>  #>      period_days("2024-01-01", "2024-12-31") # a leap year #>      period_days("2023-01-01", "2023-12-31") #>      period_days("2025-04-01", "2026-03-31") # a fiscal year #>       #>      # a quarter as the period of an average daily population #>      adp(4200, t = period_days(as.Date("2025-01-01"), as.Date("2025-03-31"))) #>       #>      # numbers are not dates, and the end cannot come first #>      try(period_days(1, 31)) #>      try(period_days("2024-12-31", "2024-01-01")) #>        # capture the output instead of printing it lines <- character() status <- bricklayer_cli(c("functions", "^drbg_"),                          out = function(x) lines <<- c(lines, x)) status #> [1] 0 lines #> [1] "  drbg_generate  Draw bytes from a DRBG
"                                                   #> [2] "  drbg_new       A deterministic random bit generator: AES-256 CTR_DRBG (NIST SP 800-90A)
" #> [3] "  drbg_reseed    Reseed a DRBG
"                                                             # an unknown verb is a usage error: status 2, nothing run bricklayer_cli("nonsense") #> rmoriebricklayer: unknown verb 'nonsense'; try `rmoriebricklayer help`, or `rmoriebricklayer ask "QUESTION"` for a model

(1952 bytes) #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  # a verifier needs the attestation and the manifest, nothing else res <- capsule_check_attestation(att, m) res$ok #> [1] TRUE res$checks #>                  check   ok #> 1 attestation_complete TRUE #> 2      manifest_digest TRUE #> 3            signature TRUE #>                                                             detail #> 1                                                                  #> 2 efa1b7387f225380245de0b5170999e87ad4044f3e8fd2ef6a6bfbc2bd0a9c90 #> 3                                                                   # any change to the manifest breaks it m2 <- m m2$meta$rows <- 1201L capsule_check_attestation(att, m2)$ok #> [1] FALSE  # and so does presenting a different key capsule_check_attestation(att, m,   key_expected = fips_keygen("ML-DSA-65")$public )$ok #> [1] FALSE  # the note is signed too: editing it breaks the signature row forged <- att forged$note <- "counts corrected" capsule_check_attestation(forged, m)$checks[, c("check", "ok")] #>                  check    ok #> 1 attestation_complete  TRUE #> 2      manifest_digest  TRUE #> 3            signature FALSE  # a context string and a pre-hash att2 <- capsule_attest(m, key, context = "release 2026-10", prehash = "sha512") capsule_check_attestation(att2, m, key_expected = key)$ok #> [1] TRUE  # a key that is not a signing key is refused try(capsule_attest(m, "not-a-key")) #> Error : `key` must come from fips_keygen() or pqc_keygen()

code: set.seed(5) ref <- data.frame(   value = stats::rnorm(300),   size = stats::runif(300, 1, 10),   grade = sample(c("a", "b", "c"), 300, TRUE) )  # A fresh draw from the same process: no drift. same <- data.frame(   value = stats::rnorm(300),   size = stats::runif(300, 1, 10),   grade = sample(c("a", "b", "c"), 300, TRUE) ) d <- capsule_drift(ref, same) d$any_drift #> [1] FALSE  # A silently rescaled column, and a new category, are both caught. moved <- same moved$size <- moved$size * 3 moved$grade[1:100] <- "z" capsule_drift(ref, moved) #> ── Capsule drift report ────────────────────────────────────────── #>   ✗ DRIFT DETECTED #>  #>   reference rows  300 #>   current rows    300 #>   columns tested  3 #>   alpha           0.01 #>  #> ── Per-column tests ────────────────────────────────────────────── #>      column        type  stat      p   psi #>    ✗   size     numeric 0.743 <2e-16 4.299 #>    ✗  grade categorical   121 <2e-16 4.381 #>    ✓  value     numeric  0.05  0.847 0.092 #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  # The PSI is always reported as an effect size, but on a sample this # small it is not allowed to raise the flag by itself -- binning noise # alone would clear 0.25. Lower psi_min_n to override that. capsule_drift(ref, same)$columns$psi #> [1] 0.092442043 0.066359848 0.003317333  # Structural changes are reported rather than tested. capsule_drift(ref, same[, c("value", "grade")])$removed #> [1] "size"  try(capsule_drift(ref, as.matrix(same))) #> Error : `reference` and `current` must both be data frames

code: set.seed(1) d <- data.frame(x = rnorm(120), y = rnorm(120)) # inject a linear effect of x on y inj <- function(z, size) {   z$y <- z$y + size * z$x   z } pw <- capsule_power(d, function(z) cor(z$x, z$y), inj,                     sizes = c(0, 0.3, 0.6), treatment = "x",                     n = 99, reps = 5, seed = 42) pw$curve #>   size detected reps rate #> 1  0.0        0    5    0 #> 2  0.3        5    5    1 #> 3  0.6        5    5    1 pw #> ── Positive controls: an injected effect of known size ─────────── #>   99 permutations, 5 repetition(s) per size, alpha 0.05 #> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #>   size 0          detected  0/5   rate 0.00 #>   size 0.3        detected  5/5   rate 1.00 #>   size 0.6        detected  5/5   rate 1.00 #> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── #>   smallest size detected at a rate of 0.8: 0.3 #>   a null result is informative only about effects at least this #>   large; smaller ones would have been missed #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  # The rate at size 0 estimates the false-positive rate. With few # repetitions it is usually 0, because alpha is small -- five draws # at 0.05 come up empty about three times in four -- so read it as a # sanity check that it is not LARGE, not as an estimate of alpha. pw$curve[pw$curve$size == 0, "rate"] #> [1] 0  # an injection with fresh noise each time, and smaller effects inj2 <- function(z, size) {   z$y <- z$y + size * z$x + stats::rnorm(nrow(z), sd = 0.5)   z } capsule_power(d, function(z) cor(z$x, z$y), inj2, sizes = c(0.1, 0.2),               treatment = "x", n = 49, reps = 4, seed = 7)$smallest_detected #> [1] NA  # too few permutations to ever reach alpha = 0.05 try(capsule_power(d, function(z) cor(z$x, z$y), inj, treatment = "x", n = 9)) #> Error : with 9 permutations the smallest p-value is 0.1, which is above alpha = 0.05: no size could ever be detected

code: set.seed(1) ref <- data.frame(   id = 1:200,   score = stats::runif(200, 0, 10),   grade = sample(c("a", "b", "c"), 200, TRUE),   stringsAsFactors = FALSE )  # A fresh extract from the same process: nothing to report. cur <- ref cur$score <- stats::runif(200, 0, 10) capsule_report(cur, reference = ref, schema = infer_schema(ref)) #> ── Capsule report ──────────────────────────────────────────────── #>   ✓ these checks found nothing #>  #>   rows           200 #>   columns        3 #>   missing cells  0.0% #>   complete rows  100.0% #>   digest         5d70a73bdcbc84111491db56743c94fd #>  #>   No finding is proof of correctness: each check has a #>   stated blind spot, and a small sample has little power. #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  # code: op <- options(rmoriebricklayer.xmss_index_file = tempfile())  # keep this example's # one-time index record out of your configuration directory; leave the default in use # Symmetric: one shared secret. sig <- capsule_sign("sha256:abc123", key = "shared-secret",                     scheme = "hmac") capsule_verify("sha256:abc123", sig, "shared-secret") #> [1] TRUE capsule_verify("sha256:TAMPERED", sig, "shared-secret") #> [1] FALSE  # Post-quantum: the verifier needs only the public root. key <- pqc_keygen(height = 2) s1 <- capsule_sign("manifest-1", key) capsule_verify("manifest-1", s1, signing_public_key(key)) #> [1] TRUE  # Advance the key past the signature before signing again. key <- xmss_advance(key, s1) key$next_index #> [1] 1 s2 <- capsule_sign("manifest-2", key) capsule_verify("manifest-2", s2, signing_public_key(key)) #> [1] TRUE  # A signature does not transfer to another message. capsule_verify("manifest-1", s2, signing_public_key(key)) #> [1] FALSE  # A standardised key: no state, any number of signatures. fk <- fips_keygen("ML-DSA-44") s3 <- capsule_sign("manifest-3", fk, context = "release", deterministic = TRUE) capsule_verify("manifest-3", s3, fips_public_key(fk), context = "release") #> [1] TRUE  # An XMSS signature needs an XMSS key. try(capsule_sign("manifest-4", "shared-secret", scheme = "xmss")) #> Error : `scheme = "xmss"` needs a key from pqc_keygen() options(op)

code: op <- options(rmoriebricklayer.xmss_index_file = tempfile())  # keep this example's # one-time index record out of your configuration directory; leave the default in use key <- pqc_keygen(height = 2) sig <- capsule_sign("pinned-manifest", key) pub <- signing_public_key(key)  capsule_verify("pinned-manifest", sig, pub) #> [1] TRUE  # Every way of being wrong returns FALSE. capsule_verify("edited-manifest", sig, pub)              # message changed #> [1] FALSE bad <- sig; bad$signature <- paste0("ff", substring(bad$signature, 3)) capsule_verify("pinned-manifest", bad, pub)              # signature edited #> [1] FALSE capsule_verify("pinned-manifest", sig,                signing_public_key(pqc_keygen(height = 2)))  # foreign key #> [1] FALSE  # A truncated signature is not verified, and does not error. trunc <- sig; trunc$signature <- substring(sig$signature, 1, 64) capsule_verify("pinned-manifest", trunc, pub) #> [1] FALSE  # HMAC: the verifier holds the same secret. tag <- capsule_sign("pinned-manifest", "shared-secret", scheme = "hmac") capsule_verify("pinned-manifest", tag, "shared-secret") #> [1] TRUE  # Something that is not a signature at all is an error, not FALSE. try(capsule_verify("pinned-manifest", list(signature = "00"), pub)) #> Error : `signature` must come from capsule_sign() options(op)

title: Bootstrap replicate means (C backend) — core_bootstrap_mean
text: Replicate \(b\) draws \(n\) indices uniformly \(1, \dots, n\) replacement (C++ std::mt19937_64 seeded seed, std::uniform_int_distribution, whose algorithm C++ library's , replicates seed can differ libstdc++ libc++) returns mean drawn values, accumulated extended precision. replicates single stream: first B replicates seed whatever larger B asked later. Edge cases: empty x gives B values NaN; NA x makes every replicate draws NA, remove missing values first. B must whole number least 1 ("B must single whole number >= 1"); character, factor list x refused ("must numeric"). seed must whole number 0 \(2^{53}\): NA, negative fractional seed refused. Performance: work \(B \times n\) draws (0.4 s \(B = 2000\), \(n = 20000\) laptop). kernel polls Ctrl-C every million draws, long run can interrupted; runs, interactive session (one options(morie.progress = TRUE)) shows spinner stderr 0.75 s , options(morie.quiet = TRUE) silences .

title: Bootstrap replicate means (C backend) — core_bootstrap_mean
code: set.seed(1) x <- stats::rnorm(50, mean = 5)  reps <- core_bootstrap_mean(x, B = 500, seed = 7) length(reps) #> [1] 500  # The replicates centre on the sample mean, and their spread estimates # the standard error. c(sample = mean(x), bootstrap = mean(reps)) #>    sample bootstrap  #>  5.100448  5.097066  c(bootstrap_se = stats::sd(reps),   formula_se = stats::sd(x) / sqrt(length(x))) #> bootstrap_se   formula_se  #>    0.1174288    0.1175769   # A percentile confidence interval for the mean. stats::quantile(reps, c(0.025, 0.975)) #>     2.5%    97.5%  #> 4.864298 5.311439   # Reproducible: the same seed gives the same replicates, and R's own # random stream is not consumed. identical(core_bootstrap_mean(x, 100, seed = 1),           core_bootstrap_mean(x, 100, seed = 1)) #> [1] TRUE  # A longer run continues the same stream. identical(core_bootstrap_mean(x, 10, seed = 1),           core_bootstrap_mean(x, 100, seed = 1)[1:10]) #> [1] TRUE  # At least one replicate is needed. try(core_bootstrap_mean(x, B = 0)) #> Error : `B` must be a single whole number >= 1

title: Hawkes-process negative log-likelihood (C backend) — core_hawkes_nll
text:
Four triggering kernels available. "exponential" memoryless evaluates O(n) recursion; three , cost O(n^2). Parameters passed scales kernel defined : par = c(a0, eta, ...) a0 LOG baseline intensity ( \(
u = e^{a0}\)) eta branching ratio (0, 1) – expected number children per event, process stationary eta < 1. remaining entries kernel's shape parameters: beta (exponential), alpha, lambda (Weibull: shape scale), alpha, c (Lomax: shape scale, \(g(u) = \alpha c^\alpha (u + c)^{-(\alpha + 1)}\)), alpha, beta (gamma: shape rate). likelihood core_hawkes_fit() maximises, parameters. conditional intensity \(\lambda(t) = 
u + \eta \sum_{t_i < t} g(t - t_i)\) \(g\) probability density \((0, \infty)\) (\(\eta\) branching ratio), value returned $$-\ell = -\sum_i \log \lambda(t_i) + \int_0^T \lambda(t)\,dt,$$ \(T\) = horizon (Hawkes, 1971). exponential kernel \(g(u) =  eta e^{- eta u}\). events value compensator alone, \(
u T\). feasible region, outside sentinel 1e12 returned instead value: \(-20 < a_0 < 20\); \(10^{-6} < \eta < 0.999\); kernel parameters, exponential \(0.05 \le  eta \le 30\); Weibull shape \([0.05, 20]\) scale \([0.001, 1000]\); Lomax shape \([0.05, 30]\) scale \([0.001, 100]\); gamma shape \([0.05, 20]\) rate \([0.05, 30]\). missing parameter also gives sentinel. Refusals (errors, sentinel): times missing value, sorted, outside \([0, T]\); horizon single positive finite number; kernel among four; par wrong length kernel. quadratic kernels poll Ctrl-C run, long evaluation can interrupted.

title: Hawkes-process negative log-likelihood (C backend) — core_hawkes_nll
code: set.seed(4) times <- sort(stats::runif(40, 0, 10))  # Exponential kernel: log-baseline -0.5, branching 0.3, decay 1.2. core_hawkes_nll(times, 10, "exponential", c(-0.5, 0.3, 1.2)) #> [1] -1.8753  # Lower is better, so this is what an optimiser minimises. nll <- function(p) core_hawkes_nll(times, 10, "exponential", p) fit <- stats::optim(c(-0.5, 0.3, 1.2), nll) fit$par #> [1] 1.03407757 0.99899989 0.08854609  # A branching ratio at or above 1 is not a stationary process, and is # reported as the infeasible sentinel rather than a number. core_hawkes_nll(times, 10, "exponential", c(-0.5, 1.5, 1.2)) == 1e12 #> [1] TRUE  # The heavier-tailed kernels take two shape parameters. core_hawkes_nll(times, 10, "gamma", c(-0.5, 0.3, 2, 1.5)) #> [1] -1.550628  # Unsorted times are an error, not the sentinel. try(core_hawkes_nll(rev(times), 10, "exponential", c(-0.5, 0.3, 1.2))) #> Error : `times` must be sorted in increasing order

text: mean \(\bar x_w = \sum_i w_i x_i / \sum_i w_i\). weights treated RELIABILITY weights (precisely observation known), variance $$s_w^2 = \frac{\sum_i w_i (x_i - \bar x_w)^2}   {\sum_i w_i - \sum_i w_i^2 / \sum_i w_i},$$ unbiased estimator reading. every weight equal 1 reduces exactly stats::var(). text: model \(\log \mu_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 (x_t - \bar x) + \log o_t\), \(o_t\) offset (1 none), fitted iteratively reweighted least squares (50 iterations). rate ratio \(e^{\beta_1}\), Wald interval \(e^{\beta_1 \pm z\, \mathrm{se}}\). dispersion reported Poisson fit assumes one. code: # A count falling by about 15% a year. set.seed(3) y <- stats::rpois(8, lambda = 200 * 0.85^(0:7)) fit <- count_trend(y) round(fit$rate_ratio, 3) #> [1] 0.869 c(fit$lower, fit$upper) #> [1] 0.8444785 0.8942357  # With a varying denominator the trend is in the rate. count_trend(c(20, 25, 30), offset = c(1000, 1500, 2500))$rate_ratio #> [1] 0.7708656  # Counts that swing far more than Poisson noise get the wider interval. wild <- count_trend(c(10, 50, 5, 60, 8, 70)) wild$dispersion #> [1] 26.27417 wild$method #> [1] "quasi-Poisson (dispersion above 1.5)"  try(count_trend(c(1.5, 2, 3))) #> Error : `y` must be non-negative whole numbers

code: set.seed(1) n <- 200 df <- data.frame(height = stats::rnorm(n, 170, 10)) df$weight <- df$height * 0.5 + stats::rnorm(n, 0, 5)  # A row that is ordinary on each variable but unlikely jointly: # short and heavy. df[1, ] <- list(height = 155, weight = 100)  out <- mahalanobis_outliers(df) head(out, 3) #> ── Mahalanobis outliers (robust) ─────────────────────────────────  #>   ! 1 of 3 rows beyond alpha = 0.001 #>  #>  row distance  p_value log_p_value outlier #>    1     4.30 9.61e-05   -9.249997    TRUE #>   32     2.90   0.0149   -4.204956   FALSE #>   14     2.81   0.0194   -3.940191   FALSE #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────   # It is flagged, although both values lie inside the other rows' ranges. out$row[1] == 1 #> [1] TRUE range(df$height[-1]) #> [1] 147.8530 194.0162 range(df$weight[-1]) #> [1]  67.07546 101.82631  # A cluster of bad rows drags the mean toward itself; the median and # MAD move less, so the robust distance of such a row is the larger. bad <- df bad[2:21, ] <- list(height = 150, weight = 110) d_classical <- mahalanobis_outliers(bad, robust = FALSE) d_robust <- mahalanobis_outliers(bad, robust = TRUE) d_classical$distance[d_classical$row == 2] < d_robust$distance[d_robust$row == 2] #> [1] TRUE  # A duplicated column has no distance defined, and is refused. dup <- df dup$height2 <- dup$height try(mahalanobis_outliers(dup)) #> Error : the columns are collinear, so no Mahalanobis distance is defined. Drop the redundant column(s) -- drop_constant() and top_correlations() will find them.

title: Little's test for data missing completely at random — mcar_test
code: set.seed(1) n <- 300 x <- stats::rnorm(n) y <- x + stats::rnorm(n)  # Missing completely at random: a coin flip decides, so the test # should not reject. mcar <- data.frame(x = x, y = y) mcar$y[sample(n, 90)] <- NA mcar_test(mcar) #> ── Little's MCAR test ──────────────────────────────────────────── #>   ✓ no departure from MCAR detected #>  #>   statistic      1.094 #>   df             1 #>   p-value        0.296 #>   patterns       2 #>   variables      2 #>   rows used      300 #>   EM iterations  13 #>  #>   Not evidence OF MCAR: a large p-value is a failure to detect a #>   departure, and this test has little power on small samples. #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  # Missing depending on the OTHER, observed variable: not MCAR, and # detectable, because the pattern's mean of x is shifted. mar <- data.frame(x = x, y = y) mar$y[x > 0.4] <- NA mcar_test(mar) #> ── Little's MCAR test ──────────────────────────────────────────── #>   ✗ MCAR rejected: the missingness is related to the data #>  #>   statistic      180.118 #>   df             1 #>   p-value        <2e-16 #>   patterns       2 #>   variables      2 #>   rows used      300 #>   EM iterations  69 #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  # Complete data has one pattern and nothing to test. mcar_test(data.frame(a = x, b = y))$df #> [1] 0  # A duplicated column makes the likelihood degenerate, and is refused. dup <- mcar dup$x2 <- dup$x try(mcar_test(dup)) #> Error : the columns are collinear (or one is constant), so the multivariate normal likelihood Little's test is built on is degenerate. Drop the redundant column(s) first -- top_correlations() and drop_constant() will find them.  # The EM estimates are the ML ones: with no missingness they are the # column means and the ML (1/n) covariance. fit <- mcar_test(data.frame(a = x, b = y)) all.equal(fit$mu, c(mean(x), mean(y)), check.attributes = FALSE) #> [1] TRUE

text: Labels lower-cased trimmed; Unicode dash family (U+2010 U+2015 minus sign U+2212) read hyphen, correctly grouped thousands separators removed ("1,000 2,499"). , order: Closed range: two numbers joined , - , optionally preceded one word followed unit ("ages 18-24", "0 5 overnight stays"). two numbers must numbers label, lower must exceed upper, open-band cue word (, , , less, plus, ...) + may appear; otherwise label NA. Open upper band, inclusive: "50+", "65 ", "", "", "", "plus". lower bound number closed_upper = TRUE, number plus one step otherwise. Open upper band, exclusive: "greater ", "", "", "", "gt". lower bound number plus one step. Open lower band, inclusive: "17 ", "less", "fewer", "", "". upper bound number. Open lower band, exclusive: "less ", "fewer ", "", "", "<", "lt". upper bound number minus one step. Bare number: band width zero. bare negative number ("-5") read suppressed cell stays NA. step 1 integer_scale = TRUE label decimal point, 0 otherwise. label one number range, empty label NA give NA bounds. Anything character factor vector error.

title: Atmospheric dispersion: sigmas, plume rise, plume, puff, grid and particles — pg_sigmas
text: pg_sigmas(): Briggs (1973) fits Pasquill-Gifford dispersion coefficients stability class -F, rural sigma_y = a_y x (1 + 0.0001 x)^(-1/2) (urban: 0.0004) sigma_z = a_z x (1 + b_z x)^(e_z). briggs_plume_rise(): buoyancy flux F = g v_s d^2 (T_s - T_a) / (4 T_s); final rise 21.425 F^(3/4) / u x_f = 49 F^(5/8) F < 55, else 38.71 F^(3/5) / u x_f = 119 F^(2/5), classes -D; 2.6 (F / (u s))^(1/3) s = g (dtheta/dz) / T_a x_f = 2.0715 u / sqrt(s) E F; transitional rise 1.6 F^(1/3) x^(2/3) / u x_f (EPA ISC3). gaussian_plume(): Q / (2 pi u sigma_y sigma_z) exp(-y^2 / (2 sigma_y^2)) V, V vertical term ground reflection , mixing lid, n_images pairs image terms. gaussian_puff(): instantaneous release sigma_x = sigma_y evaluated travel distance u t. advection_diffusion_2d(): explicit upwind advection, central diffusion, forward Euler, zero boundaries. explicit scheme stable |u dt/dx| + |v dt/dy| + 2 (kx dt/dx^2 + ky dt/dy^2) <= 1 (von Neumann bound upwind advection forward-time centred-space diffusion); sum returned stability_number stable. call outside bound run given: step split enough sub-steps smaller dt satisfy (reported substeps dt), warning, field solution physical time rather numerical explosion. separate cfl diffusion_number reported reference; 1 necessary, sufficient. lagrangian_particles(): random walk x + u dt + sqrt(2 K dt) xi (Thomson 1987) optional counting grid. stability classes run "" (unstable, sunny light wind) "D" (neutral, overcast windy) "F" (stable, clear night light wind). Units SI: metres, seconds, kelvin; q g/s, gaussian_plume() returns g/m^3, mass g, gaussian_puff() returns g/m^3. plume defined upwind source: receptor \(x \le 0\) gets 0. plume's h effective height, stack height plus rise briggs_plume_rise(). Every physical input checked: emission rates, masses, heights distances non-negative, wind speed, travel time grid steps positive, n_images whole number 1,000, stack hot air hotter (temperatures 150 refused probably Celsius), x0, y0 single numbers; release mixing_height warns, receptor ground lid (reflection terms give mirror values ). Unknown stability classes settings errors. Cost: gaussian_plume() gaussian_puff() fast thousands receptors. advection_diffusion_2d() R loop roughly 0.8 million cell updates second, grid models refuse run max_work cell particle updates. particle walk reproducible seed touch R's random number stream. Progress bars shown interactive session.

rise of a hot plume, and the effective height it gives a 50 m stack rise <- briggs_plume_rise(c(100, 1000), u = 4, diameter = 1, exit_velocity = 12,                           stack_temp = 420, ambient_temp = 285) rise$rise #> [1] 18.22335 28.88281 h_eff <- 50 + rise$final_rise  # ground-level concentration (g/m^3) from 100 g/s along the centreline rec <- cbind(x = c(500, 1000, 2000, 8000), y = 0, z = 0) gaussian_plume(100, u = 4, h = h_eff, receptors = rec) #> [1] 2.120279e-05 3.168716e-04 3.826280e-04 1.051326e-04  # title: Cross-fitted partially linear regression (double machine learning) — plr_crossfit
text: partially linear model \(Y = \theta D + g(X) + U\), \(D = m(X) + V\) Chernozhukov et al. (2018, section 4.2), estimated DML2 cross-fitting recipe: sample split k_folds folds; fold nuisances \(m\) \(g\) fitted folds predicted ; \(\hat\theta\) slope --fold outcome residuals --fold treatment residuals, $$\hat\theta = \sum_i \hat V_i \hat U_i / \sum_i \hat V_i^2,$$ sandwich standard error \(\sqrt{\sum_i \hat V_i^2 (\hat U_i - \hat\theta \hat V_i)^2} / \sum_i \hat V_i^2\). nuisances ordinary least squares covariates, right learner confounding approximately linear keeps estimator fully deterministic given seed; rmorie's morie_estimate_double_ml() offers richer learners can passed exposure_response_plr estimator. fold's two least-squares fits computed normal equations covariates centred scaled full-sample moments (column space, fitted values lm.fit), solved Cholesky; fold whose cross-product poorly conditioned (reciprocal condition number 1e-5: collinear covariates constant column) uses lm.fit instead, whose pivoting drops redundant columns (coefficients count 0). n = 20000 fit takes milliseconds. bar stderr shows folds work slow enough need one (see bricklayer_progress). Rows missing value named columns dropped first (n reports rows used). folds random permutation rep_len(1:k_folds, n) drawn seed; R's random stream restored afterwards. Refusals: column name single string (several covariates) data; non-numeric column (factor code); k_folds whole number least 2; fewer 2 * k_folds complete rows; treatment variation left covariates partialled .

title: Cross-fitted partially linear regression (double machine learning) — plr_crossfit
text: Chernozhukov, V., Chetverikov, D., Demirer, M., Duflo, E., Hansen, C., Newey, W. Robins, J. (2018). Double/debiased machine learning treatment structural parameters. Econometrics Journal 21(1), C1-C68.

title: Cross-fitted partially linear regression (double machine learning) — plr_crossfit
code: set.seed(1) d <- data.frame(x1 = rnorm(200), x2 = rnorm(200)) d$exposure <- 20 + 2 * d$x1 + rnorm(200) d$asthma <- 5 + 0.3 * d$exposure + d$x2 + rnorm(200) fit <- plr_crossfit(d, "asthma", "exposure", c("x1", "x2")) fit$ate #> [1] 0.2536464  # A 95 percent normal confidence interval from the standard error. fit$ate + c(-1.96, 1.96) * fit$se #> [1] 0.1156209 0.3916718  # The fold split changes the estimate a little; ten folds instead of five. plr_crossfit(d, "asthma", "exposure", c("x1", "x2"), k_folds = 10, seed = 2)$ate #> [1] 0.2676102  # A text column is refused rather than read as codes. d$region <- sample(c("north", "south"), 200, replace = TRUE) try(plr_crossfit(d, "asthma", "exposure", c("x1", "region"))) #> Error : column `region` must be numeric (a factor or character column is not a code)

code: f <- factor(c("W", "B", "O", "W")) relabel(f, c(W = "White", B = "Black", O = "Other")) #> [1] White Black Other White #> attr(,"recode_audit") #> attr(,"recode_audit")$mapping #>     W     B     O  #> White Black Other  #>  #> attr(,"recode_audit")$kept #> character(0) #>  #> attr(,"recode_audit")$checksum #> [1] 992b6c4a35a3cea9e5875c90f562a3259fe9f08f1eb2fac9754d7c5b5f52bdd3 #>  #> Levels: White Black Other  # the level order follows the mapping, not the alphabet levels(relabel(f, c(W = "White", O = "Other", B = "Black"))) #> [1] "White" "Other" "Black"  # a kept label passes through relabel(c("W", "B", "X"), c(W = "White", B = "Black"), keep = "X") #> [1] White Black X     #> attr(,"recode_audit") #> attr(,"recode_audit")$mapping #>     W     B  #> White Black  #>  #> attr(,"recode_audit")$kept #> [1] X #>  #> attr(,"recode_audit")$checksum #> [1] ec818263ffb31defd682d27e1321fa8ea63f3f231b36b6b99fba61dca9510602 #>  #> Levels: White Black X  # positional labels are refused try(relabel(f, c("Black", "Other", "White"))) #> Error : relabel: `mapping` must be NAMED (old label = new label). Assigning labels by POSITION is how four race codes were rotated in a published analysis (OHRC correction, 26 January 2023): the labels were in alphabetical order, the codes were not.

title: Name the mechanical step that reproduces a label permutation — relabel_forensics
code: # the OHRC 2023 case: alphabetical labels assigned to codes 1-4 vl <- c("1" = "White", "2" = "Black", "3" = "Other", "4" = "Unknown") obs <- c(White = "Black", Black = "Other", Other = "Unknown",          Unknown = "White") relabel_forensics(vl, obs) #> Mechanism(s) reproducing the observed permutation: #>   * labels sorted alphabetically, assigned by code position #>       White -> Black, Black -> Other, Other -> Unknown, Unknown -> White #>   * labels sorted case-insensitively, assigned by code position #>       White -> Black, Black -> Other, Other -> Unknown, Unknown -> White #>   * rotation by 1 position(s) #>       White -> Black, Black -> Other, Other -> Unknown, Unknown -> White #>  #> The observed permutation is reproduced EXACTLY by: labels sorted alphabetically, assigned by code position; labels sorted case-insensitively, assigned by code position; rotation by 1 position(s). No import routine (haven, foreign, pandas, pyreadstat) reorders value labels; each carries them keyed by code. A transfer fault does not select the sort order of the labels. The step that did this was a positional relabel in the analysis, and it is reproducible from the code book alone.  # a frequency-ordered relabel needs the counts obs2 <- c(White = "White", Black = "Other", Other = "Black",           Unknown = "Unknown") rf <- relabel_forensics(vl, obs2, counts = c(White = 50, Black = 10,                                              Other = 30, Unknown = 5)) rf$mechanism[rf$matches] #> [1] "labels ordered by decreasing frequency, assigned by code position"  # observed must be a permutation of the labels try(relabel_forensics(vl, c(White = "Black"))) #> Error : relabel_forensics: `observed` must be a permutation of the labels in `value_labels`

text: bricklayer_json_base64_enc() breaks output 72-character lines (newline complete block 54 input bytes), matching jsonlite's encoder byte byte; decoder ignores line breaks, white space = padding, either form round trips. character outside alphabet error rather skipped, skipping decode corrupted body shorter valid-looking one. title: Base64 encoding — rmbl_base64
code: # Round trip through the standard alphabet. b <- bricklayer_json_base64_enc("hello capsule") b #> [1] "aGVsbG8gY2Fwc3VsZQ==" rawToChar(bricklayer_json_base64_dec(b)) #> [1] "hello capsule"  # Raw input works the same way. bricklayer_json_base64_enc(charToRaw("abc")) #> [1] "YWJj" bricklayer_json_base64_dec(bricklayer_json_base64_enc(charToRaw("abc"))) #> [1] 61 62 63  # Padding appears when the length is not a multiple of three. bricklayer_json_base64_enc("a") #> [1] "YQ==" bricklayer_json_base64_enc("ab") #> [1] "YWI=" bricklayer_json_base64_enc("abc") #> [1] "YWJj"  # The URL-safe variant has no "+", "/" or "=" to escape. bricklayer_json_base64url_enc(as.raw(c(255, 224, 63))) #> [1] "_-A_" bricklayer_json_base64_enc(as.raw(c(255, 224, 63))) #> [1] "/+A/" bricklayer_json_base64url_dec(   bricklayer_json_base64url_enc("path/safe?yes") ) #>  [1] 70 61 74 68 2f 73 61 66 65 3f 79 65 73  # Long input is wrapped, and the decoder ignores the breaks. long <- bricklayer_json_base64_enc(strrep("x", 200)) grepl("\n", long) #> [1] TRUE rawToChar(bricklayer_json_base64_dec(long)) == strrep("x", 200) #> [1] TRUE  # A character outside the alphabet is refused, not skipped. try(bricklayer_json_base64_dec("ab$c")) #> Error : base64 input contains characters outside the alphabet

Conversely, truncating END leaves perfectly valid prefix chain_verify() accepts, head changes. two failures complementary, chain_seal() exists: verifies links folds entry count every link digest one value (SHA-256 count links joined "|"), single signature seal detects edit, deletion, reordering, insertion truncation alike. code: op <- options(rmoriebricklayer.xmss_index_file = tempfile())  # keep this example's # one-time index record out of your configuration directory; leave the default in use ch <- chain_new() ch <- chain_append(ch, "manifest for run 1", label = "run-1") ch <- chain_append(ch, "manifest for run 2", label = "run-2") ch <- chain_append(ch, "manifest for run 3", label = "run-3") ch #> ── Manifest chain ──────────────────────────────────────────────── #>   ✓ chain intact #>  #>   entries  3 #>   head     b9ccb96106a68f3d4d2a0cfb8e2ae160f7996393e28e93d7f4650c2bbd81ff49 #>   seal     940721e3704268b570bcbf1c9ae841bde02927f584ec44dc3cf053ef7404d8a0 #>  #>     1  run-1            cb25fa776c693a106b2d08a1 #>     2  run-2            03a645a531c93fbb12bb2c07 #>     3  run-3            b9ccb96106a68f3d4d2a0cfb #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  # An intact chain verifies. chain_verify(ch)$valid #> [1] TRUE  # Editing an entry breaks it, and names where. edited <- ch edited$entries[[2]]$digest <- core_sha256("something else") chain_verify(edited)$valid #> [1] FALSE chain_verify(edited)$broken_at #> [1] 2  # So does deleting one, which a per-manifest digest would not catch. dropped <- ch dropped$entries[[2]] <- NULL chain_verify(dropped)$valid #> [1] FALSE  # Sign the SEAL, which covers the links and the length together. key <- pqc_keygen(height = 2) sig <- capsule_sign(chain_seal(ch), key) capsule_verify(chain_seal(ch), sig, signing_public_key(key)) #> [1] TRUE  # Truncating the chain still seals, but to a different value, so the # signature no longer verifies. truncated <- ch truncated$entries[[3]] <- NULL capsule_verify(chain_seal(truncated), sig, signing_public_key(key)) #> [1] FALSE  # A chain whose links disagree has no seal to present at all. chain_seal(dropped) #> [1] NA  # any object can be an entry, such as a whole manifest list ch2 <- chain_append(chain_new(), list(run = 1, mean = 2.5), label = "list entry") chain_head(ch2) #> [1] "05bb042d04eb7378d536c4197e61f280f2e9f99d33d0c9cc28a475c488a4a206"  # only chains are accepted try(chain_verify(list(entries = list()))) #> Error : `chain` must come from chain_new() options(op)

code: x <- c(2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9) core_quantile(x, c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75)) #> 25% 50% 75%  #> 4.0 4.5 5.5  all.equal(core_quantile(x, c(0.1, 0.9)),           as.numeric(stats::quantile(x, c(0.1, 0.9)))) #> [1] "names for target but not for current"  core_median(x) #> [1] 4.5 core_mad(x) #> [1] 0.7413 all.equal(core_mad(x), stats::mad(x)) #> [1] TRUE core_mad(x, constant = 1)                  # unscaled median deviation #> [1] 0.5 core_mad(x, constant = 1 / stats::qnorm(3/4))  # unrounded constant #> [1] 0.7413011  core_iqr(x) #> [1] 1.5 core_tukey_fences(x) #> lower upper  #>  1.75  7.75   # Robustness: one wild value barely moves the median, but moves the # mean a long way. wild <- c(x, 1000) c(mean = mean(wild), median = core_median(wild)) #>     mean   median  #> 115.5556   5.0000   # Values outside the fences are the candidates to inspect. f <- core_tukey_fences(wild) wild[wild < f[["lower"]] | wild > f[["upper"]]] #> [1] 1000  # A missing value is not dropped: the answer is NaN. core_median(c(1, NA, 3)) #> [1] NaN  # A probability outside [0, 1] is refused. try(core_quantile(x, 1.5)) #> Error : `probs` must lie in [0, 1]

code: chunks <- c("row1,row2", "row3,row4", "row5,row6", "row7,row8")  root <- merkle_root(chunks) root #> [1] "3b1537c90e21c2e66f341b946388abbb78bf249fb433f961fba223b67141be31"  # A single chunk's root is just its own leaf digest. merkle_root("only") == core_sha256(c(as.raw(0), charToRaw("only"))) #> [1] TRUE  # The leaves are the per-chunk digests, so a diff names the culprit. before <- merkle_leaves(chunks) after <- merkle_leaves(c(chunks[1:2], "row5,row6-EDITED", chunks[4])) which(before != after) #> [1] 3  # Prove chunk 3 belongs, without holding chunks 1, 2 or 4. pr <- merkle_proof(chunks, 3) pr #> $sibling #> [1] "a1d2780e3c438372d14e12c01b280cf9be97a244adfa43671903812ca0deb88f" #> [2] "28ee5f4ac1a7a56c508b5f1b9cd5dd74abf929b3d0f2e5852280914ddef3cb88" #>  #> $side #> [1] "right" "left"  #>  #> $scheme #> [1] 2 #>  merkle_verify(chunks[3], pr, root) #> [1] TRUE  # The proof fails for a chunk that was not in the tree. merkle_verify("row5,row6-EDITED", pr, root) #> [1] FALSE  # Any change to any chunk changes the root. merkle_root(chunks) == merkle_root(c(chunks[1:3], "row7,row8 ")) #> [1] FALSE  # an odd count: the last node is promoted, so its proof has one step merkle_proof(c("a", "b", "c"), 3) #> $sibling #> [1] "b137985ff484fb600db93107c77b0365c80d78f5b429ded0fd97361d077999eb" #>  #> $side #> [1] "left" #>  #> $scheme #> [1] 2 #>   # an index past the end is refused try(merkle_proof(chunks, 5)) #> Error : `index` must be between 1 and the number of chunks  # a root pinned by 0.5.12 or earlier recomputes with scheme = 1, and its # proofs (which record no scheme) verify with a warning old <- merkle_proof(chunks, 3, scheme = 1) old$scheme <- NULL withCallingHandlers(   merkle_verify(chunks[3], old, merkle_root(chunks, scheme = 1)),   warning = function(w) invokeRestart("muffleWarning")) #> [1] TRUE

code: df <- data.frame(   id = c(1, 2, 2),   grade = c("a", "b", "z"),   score = c(5, 200, 7),   email = c("a@b.com", "nope", "c@d.org"),   day = c(3, 1, 2),   stringsAsFactors = FALSE )  rules <- list(   rule_unique("id", severity = "fatal"),   rule_in_set("grade", c("a", "b", "c")),   rule_between("score", 0, 100),   rule_regex("email", "^[^@]+@[^@]+\\\\.[a-z]+$"),   rule_increasing("day") ) names(validate_rules(df, rules)) #> [1] "id_unique"      "grade_in_set"   "score_between"  "email_regex"    #> [5] "day_increasing"  # Each names the rows that failed. validate_rules(df, rules)$grade_in_set$rows #> [1] 3  # Clean data passes every one of them. ok <- data.frame(   id = 1:3, grade = c("a", "b", "c"),   score = c(5, 50, 7),   email = c("a@b.com", "c@d.org", "e@f.net"),   day = 1:3, stringsAsFactors = FALSE ) length(validate_rules(ok, rules)) #> [1] 1  # A robust outlier rule: MADs from the median, not standard # deviations from the mean, so one wild value cannot hide the others. validate_rules(   data.frame(v = c(1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 900)),   rule_within_n_mads("v", 5) )$v_within_mads$rows #> [1] 6  # Whole-table rules. validate_rules(df, rule_distinct_rows()) #> list() validate_rules(df, rule_col_count(5)) #> list() validate_rules(df, rule_complete_rows()) #> list()  # NA fails only when asked to g <- data.frame(grade = c("a", NA, "b")) length(validate_rules(g, rule_in_set("grade", c("a", "b")))) #> [1] 0 validate_rules(g, rule_in_set("grade", c("a", "b"), na_pass = FALSE))$grade_in_set$rows #> [1] 2  # bounds are checked when the rule is made try(rule_between("score", 100, 0)) #> Error : need `lo` <= `hi`, both non-missing

code: r <- verify_pollution("no2", demo = TRUE) r$status #> [1] "ok" r$pipeline$paf #> [1] 0.02733115 cat(pollution_report_text(r)) #> ================================================================== #>   verify-pollution -- NO2 -> all_cause_mortality #>   data:   demo (synthetic) #> ================================================================== #>  #> Inputs #>   exposure mean:      24.261 #>   exposure prevalence:0.981 #>   baseline rate/100k: 500.00 #>   population:         1,000,000 #>   reference conc:     10 #>  #> Assumption log #>   [PASS] exposure finite and non-negative -- mean 24.26113743 vs ref 10 #>   [PASS] exposure within the concentration-response range (at most 10,000 ug/m3) -- exposure_mean=24.26114 #>   [PASS] prevalence in [0,1] -- exposure_prevalence=0.981 #>   [PASS] baseline_rate finite: zero, or between 1 and 10,000 per 100k -- baseline_rate=500 per 100k per year #>   [PASS] population finite, positive and at most 10 billion -- population=1,000,000 #>   [PASS] reference finite and non-negative -- reference=10 #>   [PASS] pollutant supported by the CRFs -- Current CRFs: NO2 (log-linear), PM2.5 (log-linear all-cause; Burnett IER for IHD and stroke). Other pollutants reject. #>  #> Concentration-response #>   RR:       1.0286 #>   source:   Huangfu & Atkinson (2020) Environ Int 144:105998; WHO (2021) Global AQ Guidelines #>  #> Attributable fraction (PAF): 0.0273  (95% CI 0.0138 to 0.0534, from the risk's limits) #>  #> Mortality displaced #>   expected avoided deaths: 136.6 #>  #> Burden of pollution #>   attributable deaths:   136.7 #>  #> Equity analysis #>   concentration index: -0.0647 #>  #> STATUS: ok  # Scalar inputs: a city of 2.8 million at a PM2.5 mean of 9. s <- verify_pollution("pm25", exposure_mean = 9, exposure_prevalence = 1,                       baseline_rate = 750, population = 2.8e6, region = "Toronto") s$pipeline$burden$attributable_cases #> [1] 510.8617 attr(s, "exit_status") #> [1] 0  # A CSV of measurements with an income column. f <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv") utils::write.csv(data.frame(exposure = c(12, 18, 25, 31, 9), income = 1:5), f,                  row.names = FALSE) verify_pollution("no2", exposure_csv = f)$pipeline$equity$concentration_index #> [1] 0.02947368  # A rate per person-year passed as per 100,000 fails an assumption ... bad <- verify_pollution("no2", exposure_mean = 20, exposure_prevalence = 1,                         baseline_rate = 0.008) bad$status #> [1] "assumption_failure" # ... and an argument it cannot use is an error report, not an R error. verify_pollution("no2")$error #> [1] "no exposure data: pass exposure_csv, or exposure_mean and exposure_prevalence, or demo = TRUE"

code: # Offline: a results file whose only failure is a page that is gone # has nothing to send again, so no keys or network are used. f <- tempfile(fileext = ".jsonl") writeLines(c(   paste0('{"url":"https://example.org/","status":"saved",',          '"timestamp":"20260101120000",',          '"snapshot":"https://web.archive.org/web/20260101120000/https://example.org/",',          '"message":"","at":"2026-01-01T12:00:00Z"}'),   paste0('{"url":"https://example.org/old","status":"failed",',          '"message":"target server cannot find the page","at":"2026-01-01T12:00:00Z"}') ), f) res <- wayback_retry(f, lookup = FALSE) res #> ── Wayback Machine captures ──────────────────────────────────────  #>   2 URLs: 1 saved, 0 existing, 1 failed #>  #>  status      timestamp                     url #>   saved 20260101120000    https://example.org/ #>  failed           <NA> https://example.org/old #> ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  attr(res, "retry") #>   failed found_by_lookup captured_again left_as_gone left_for_tomorrow #> 1      1               0              0            1                 0  try(wayback_retry(tempfile(fileext = ".jsonl"))) #> Error : no results file at /tmp/Rtmp8uj0YR/file1e7345208820.jsonl  # With failures to resend, keys and the network are needed. if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ res <- wayback_save(urls, output = "snapshots.jsonl") # later, or the next day once the daily capture limits have reset: res <- wayback_retry("snapshots.jsonl") attr(res, "retry") } # }

code: op <- options(rmoriebricklayer.xmss_index_file = tempfile())  # keep this example's # one-time index record out of your configuration directory; leave the default in use key <- pqc_keygen(height = 2) s1 <- capsule_sign("manifest-1", key) key <- xmss_advance(key, s1) key$next_index #> [1] 1 s2 <- capsule_sign("manifest-2", key) capsule_verify("manifest-2", s2, signing_public_key(key)) #> [1] TRUE  # With the message, the signature is verified before the key advances. key <- xmss_advance(key, s2, message = "manifest-2") key$next_index #> [1] 2  # A key regenerated from seeds is unknown to the record until registered. s <- paste(rep("ab", 32), collapse = "") k2 <- pqc_keygen(height = 1, sk_seed = s, pub_seed = s, sk_prf = s) try(capsule_sign("m", k2)) #> Error : this XMSS key is not in the used-index record on this machine, and it claims never to have signed (next_index 0): it was generated elsewhere or from given seeds, or the record was deleted. If it has never signed, register it with xmss_register_key(key); if it has, carry it forward with xmss_advance(key, its_last_signature, message), or generate a new key with pqc_keygen() invisible(xmss_register_key(k2)) capsule_verify("m", capsule_sign("m", k2), signing_public_key(k2)) #> [1] TRUE  # Reset a test key's entry so it may sign from index 0 again. xmss_forget_used_indices(k2)  # A signature that is not an XMSS signature cannot advance a key. try(xmss_advance(key, list())) #> Error : `signature` must be an XMSS signature from capsule_sign() (or the attestation, bundle or recode manifest that carries it) options(op)

The interval is exact, so a small group does not get a confident # percent it has not earned. subset(as.data.frame(y), Gender == "Female") #>   Gender EndFiscalYear value previous change pct_change                 flag #> 1 Female          2019    31       NA     NA         NA no comparison period #> 2 Female          2020    28       31     -3  -9.677419                 <NA> #> 3 Female          2021    12       28    -16 -57.142857                 <NA> #> 4 Female          2022    19       12      7  58.333333                 <NA> #> 5 Female          2023    24       19      5  26.315789                 <NA> #>   pct_lower pct_upper verdict #> 1        NA        NA    <NA> #> 2 -47.79679  55.62836  better #> 3 -80.14950 -12.97354  better #> 4 -27.02865 257.66674   worse #> 5 -33.67876 143.90121   worse  # A percentage is handled as percentage points, not as a percent of a # percent. rate <- data.frame(year = 2019:2023, share = c(4.1, 4.6, 5.2, 5.0, 5.4)) yoy(rate, value = "share", period = "year", units = "percent") #> year  share  previous  change  points   #> ────  ─────  ────────  ──────  ──────── #> 2019  4.1    —         —         —      #>     ↳ note: no comparison period #> 2020  4.6    4.1       0.5     ▲ +0.5pp #> 2021  5.2    4.6       0.6     ▲ +0.6pp #> 2022  5.0    5.2       -0.2    ▼ -0.2pp #> 2023  5.4    5.0       0.4     ▲ +0.4pp #>  #> lag 1 period · units: percent · percentage-point change, not percent of a percent  # a missing year stays a gap; a bare column name works too yoy(data.frame(year = c(2019, 2021, 2022), n = c(10, 12, 15)), value = n, period = year) #> year  n   previous  change  change %  interval      #> ────  ──  ────────  ──────  ────────  ───────────── #> 2019  10  —         —         —       —             #>     ↳ note: no comparison period #> 2020  —   10        —         —       —             #>     ↳ note: no data #> 2021  12  —         —         —       —             #>     ↳ note: no comparison period #> 2022  15  12        3       ▲ +25.0%  [-45%, +192%] #>  #> lag 1 period · units: count · 95% exact rate-ratio interval  # a quarterly series compares each quarter with the same quarter a year earlier q <- ts(c(5, 6, 7, 8, 6, 7, 9, 9), frequency = 4, start = c(2020, 1)) as.data.frame(yoy(q))[5:8, c("period", "value", "previous", "pct_change")] #>    period value previous pct_change #> 5 2021.00     6        5   20.00000 #> 6 2021.25     7        6   16.66667 #> 7 2021.50     9        7   28.57143 #> 8 2021.75     9        8   12.50000  # counts must be whole numbers try(yoy(data.frame(year = 1:3, n = c(1.5, 2, 3)), "n", "year")) #> Error : `units = "count"` needs non-negative whole numbers; use units = "continuous" for a measured quantity

code: d <- data.frame(year = 2019:2023, n = c(402, 377, 190, 268, 331)) y <- yoy(d, value = "n", period = "year")  for (ext in c("csv", "tsv", "json", "md", "html")) {   f <- file.path(tempdir(), paste0("change.", ext))   yoy_write(y, f)   cat(ext, file.size(f), "bytes\n")   unlink(f) } #> csv 482 bytes #> tsv 482 bytes #> json 1552 bytes #> md 675 bytes #> html 4828 bytes  # an extension that names no format: say which one f <- file.path(tempdir(), "change.txt") yoy_write(y, f, format = "csv", digits = 1) readLines(f, n = 3) #> [1] "# value: n; period: year; lag: 1; units: count; interval: 95% exact rate ratio" #> [2] "year,value,previous,change,pct_change,flag,pct_lower,pct_upper,verdict"         #> [3] "2019,402,,,,no comparison period,,,"                                            unlink(f) try(yoy_write(y, file.path(tempdir(), "change.xlsx"))) #> Error : cannot tell the format from "change.xlsx"; pass format = explicitly
